title: Doers, Actions, and Things
objectives: I can use the endings -er, -or, -ment, -tion, and -ion to understand new words.
I can turn a verb into a word for a person or a thing.
I can use ten noun words in my own sentences.
I can explain how an ending changes the job of a word.
rationale: Noun suffixes close the year's word-part work. Students watch verbs turn into people (invent, inventor), feelings and results (excite, excitement), and things or events (collect, collection). The ten words are all nouns built from verbs students already know. Four name people (-er and -or), four name a result or state (-ment), and two name an act or thing (-ion). Seeing that collect, collector, and collection come from one base shows students how one word can unlock a family. This is a pattern grade 4 texts use for hundreds of nouns.

words.def: A person who makes up something new for the first time.
words.ex: The inventor built a small robot that could water the plants.
words.ex2: Thomas Edison was a famous inventor who improved the light bulb.
words.nonExample: A person who only copies what others have made is not an inventor.

apps.academic: In science class, an inventor tests an idea again and again.
apps.spoken: My sister wants to be an inventor when she grows up.
apps.writing: Use inventor to name a person who makes something new.

cloze.s: The ___ spent years building a machine that could wash dishes all on its own.

cloze2.s: Alexander Graham Bell, the ___ of an early telephone, was also a teacher.

misuse.s: The inventor never made anything and only copied what others had already built.
misuse.why: An inventor makes something new, so copying other people's work does not fit.

visual.alt: A light bulb and a wrench.

words.frame: If I were an inventor, I would make ___.

words.def: A person who travels to new places to learn about them.
words.ex: The explorer packed a compass, a map, and a notebook.
words.ex2: Sacagawea helped the explorers Lewis and Clark cross the land.
words.nonExample: A person who stays home and never goes anywhere new is not an explorer.

segs.m: travel to learn about a place

morph.note: The final e of explore is dropped before -er.

apps.academic: In social studies, explorers drew maps of the places they visited.
apps.spoken: My cousin is an explorer in the woods behind her house.
apps.writing: Use explorer to name a person who travels to find something new.

cloze.s: The ___ crossed the frozen land with a map, a compass, and a team of sled dogs.

cloze2.s: A brave ___ sailed across the wide ocean in search of new lands.

misuse.s: The explorer stayed home and never went anywhere new.
misuse.why: An explorer travels to new places, so staying home does not fit.

words.def: A person who teaches a skill or a class.
words.ex: Our swimming instructor showed us how to float on our backs.
words.ex2: The art instructor handed out brushes and paper.
words.nonExample: A student who is learning to swim is not the instructor.

apps.academic: In school, an instructor explains a lesson and checks that students understand.
apps.spoken: My piano instructor taught me a new song.
apps.writing: Use instructor for a person who teaches a skill.

cloze.s: The swimming ___ showed the children how to kick and breathe.

cloze2.s: The driving ___ sat beside the new driver and pointed out each road sign.

misuse.s: The swimming instructor never taught anyone to swim and left class early.
misuse.why: An instructor teaches a skill, so never teaching does not fit.

words.frame: My instructor teaches me how to ___.

words.def: A person who gathers things of one kind as a hobby.
words.ex: My uncle is a collector of old coins.
words.ex2: The rock collector displayed shiny stones on a shelf.
words.nonExample: A person who throws away everything is not a collector.

apps.academic: In science, a rock collector sorts stones by color and how hard they are.
apps.spoken: She is a collector of postcards from all over the world.
apps.writing: Use collector for a person who saves one kind of thing.

cloze.s: The stamp ___ kept hundreds of tiny pictures from many countries in a thick album.

cloze2.s: A coin ___ paid ten dollars for a rare, old penny.

misuse.s: The collector threw away every shell and never saved anything at all.
misuse.why: A collector saves things of one kind, so throwing everything away does not fit.

visual.alt: A coin and a magnifying glass.

words.def: A strong, happy feeling when something fun is about to happen.
words.ex: The children screamed with excitement when the circus came to town.
words.ex2: Excitement filled the room on the last day of school.
words.nonExample: Feeling bored and sleepy is not excitement.

apps.academic: In stories, excitement can build before a big event.
apps.spoken: I could hardly hide my excitement at the surprise.
apps.writing: Use excitement for a strong happy feeling about something coming.

cloze.s: The class squealed with ___ when the bus arrived for the field trip.

cloze2.s: On the last day before vacation, the room was full of ___ and loud chatter.

misuse.s: She felt great excitement because nothing at all was going to happen all day.
misuse.why: Excitement is a feeling about something fun to come, so expecting nothing does not fit.

visual.alt: A party popper and a smiling face.

words.def: The fun you feel when something makes you smile or laugh.
words.ex: The clown's silly dance brought laughter and amusement to the crowd.
words.ex2: Her eyes sparkled with amusement when the puppy chased its tail.
words.nonExample: Feeling sad and tired is not amusement.

apps.academic: In stories, a character may watch with amusement as a funny thing happens.
apps.spoken: He laughed in amusement at the joke.
apps.writing: Use amusement for the light, happy feeling of finding something funny.

cloze.s: The baby giggled with ___ when her dad made a funny face.

cloze2.s: The audience laughed in ___ at the monkey's silly tricks.

misuse.s: He felt amusement when the cartoon made him cry with sadness.
misuse.why: Amusement is the fun of something funny, so crying with sadness does not fit.

visual.alt: A circus tent and a clown.

words.frame: A thing that brings me amusement is ___.

words.def: A shared promise or deal that people have said yes to.
words.ex: The two teams reached an agreement about how to share the field.
words.ex2: We shook hands to show our agreement.
words.nonExample: An argument where no one gives in is not an agreement.

segs.m: say yes to the same plan

apps.academic: In social studies, countries sign an agreement to work together.
apps.spoken: We made an agreement to take turns on the swing.
apps.writing: Use agreement for a deal or a shared plan that people accept.

cloze.s: After a long talk, the friends shook hands to show they had reached an ___.

cloze2.s: The ___ said that each student would feed the class pet on a different day.

misuse.s: The agreement was when two people argued loudly and refused to share anything.
misuse.why: An agreement is a shared deal, so refusing to share does not fit.

words.def: The care a doctor gives to help someone get better.
words.ex: The nurse gave the sick puppy treatment for its sore paw.
words.ex2: Doctors are working on a new treatment for the flu.
words.nonExample: Making someone sicker on purpose is not treatment.

apps.academic: In health class, we learn how treatment helps the body heal.
apps.spoken: The doctor's treatment cleared up my cough.
apps.writing: Use treatment for the care that helps someone recover.

cloze.s: The doctor gave the patient a ___ that helped the cough go away.

cloze2.s: The vet gave the dog ___ for its sore paw, and soon it could run again.

misuse.s: The doctor's treatment made the patient sicker on purpose.
misuse.why: Treatment is care to help someone get better, so making someone sicker does not fit.

words.def: A group of things gathered together, such as shells or stamps.
words.ex: Her shell collection fills three shelves in her bedroom.
words.ex2: The library has a large collection of picture books.
words.nonExample: One lone pebble is not a collection.

apps.academic: In science, a rock collection can be sorted by color or by how hard the rocks are.
apps.spoken: He showed us his collection of baseball cards.
apps.writing: Use collection for a group of things saved together.

cloze.s: Mia's ___ of seashells filled three shelves, and she knew where each one came from.

cloze2.s: The library's ___ includes thousands of books, maps, and magazines.

misuse.s: A collection is one single thing, such as a lone pebble in a pocket.
misuse.why: A collection is a group of things, not one single thing.

words.def: A special party or event to honor something happy.
words.ex: The town held a big celebration on the Fourth of July.
words.ex2: We planned a surprise celebration for Grandpa's birthday.
words.nonExample: A quiet afternoon with no party and nothing to honor is not a celebration.

morph.note: The final e of celebrate is dropped before -ion.

apps.academic: In social studies, we learn how families hold a celebration for special days.
apps.spoken: Our class had a celebration when we finished the book.
apps.writing: Use celebration for a party or event that honors something good.

cloze.s: Balloons, music, and a big cake made the birthday ___ one to remember.

cloze2.s: The town held a parade as part of its Fourth of July ___.

misuse.s: The celebration was a quiet afternoon with no party and nothing to honor.
misuse.why: A celebration is a party to honor something happy, so nothing to honor does not fit.

passage.title: The Pine Street Fair
paras: Mr. Alvarez was the science instructor at Pine Street School, and he had a big idea. "We will hold a fair," he told the class, "and everyone will show a favorite project." The room filled with excitement.

Ana, a young inventor, built a tiny machine that fed her fish. Her friend Ben was a rock collector, and he brought a collection of forty shiny stones, each with a label. Lila dressed as an explorer and showed a map of her own backyard.

The judges walked past each table. They laughed with amusement at Lila's map, which marked a place called the Great Swamp where her dog liked to play. Sam showed how a nurse gives treatment to a sore knee, using a bandage and a model.

Before the fair ended, the judges reached an agreement: every student would get a ribbon. Then the class held a small celebration with juice and cookies. Mr. Alvarez said it was the best Friday of the year.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "collection" most nearly means
choices: a group of things gathered together
qs.why: Ben brings forty shiny stones, each with a label, so a collection is a group of things gathered together.

qs.q: Why did the judges laugh with amusement at Lila's map?
choices: The map showed a playful, funny place, the Great Swamp, in a backyard.
qs.why: A swamp in a small backyard where a dog plays is a silly idea, so it made them smile.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the fair was fair to every student?
choices: Mr. Alvarez had a big idea.
Every student would get a ribbon.
qs.why: The judges agreed to give a ribbon to every student, so no one was left out.

qs.q: What is a central idea of the passage?
choices: Students share their projects and celebrate at a school fair.
qs.why: The story shows the fair from the idea to the celebration.

write.prompt: Write about a project, hobby, or party you know about. Use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: I want to be a ___ because ___. I would have a collection of ___.

study.task: Pick one verb from the unit, such as collect, and write the new words you can make with -or and -ion. Then use each new word in a sentence.

sentences: Write a sentence about an inventor and what the inventor made. Use because.
Write a sentence that uses both collector and collection.
Write a sentence that tells how you feel when something causes excitement.
Write a sentence about a celebration you took part in.

combine.model: Mia is a collector, and her collection of fifty seashells sits on her shelves.
The doctor's treatment helped the puppy get better.

discuss: How does the ending -or change the word invent?
What is the difference between a collector and a collection?
Which has a stronger feeling: amusement or excitement? Explain.
produce.explain: Explain how knowing the word explore helps you understand explorer and exploration.

argue.prompt: Claim: An inventor is the most important person for the future. Do you agree? Give two reasons.
argue.frame: I think an inventor ___ because ___. Another reason is ___.

constructed.prompt: Write about two people with different jobs or hobbies. Use inventor and collector.
constructed.model: An inventor builds new machines to solve problems. A collector saves old coins and keeps them in an album.

constructed.prompt: Describe a party in two sentences. Use excitement and celebration.
constructed.model: The celebration began with music and cake. The children felt excitement as the balloons floated up.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten nouns built with -er, -or, -ment, -tion, and -ion, read a story about a school fair, and practice turning verbs into nouns.

notes.va.inventor.n: Invent + -or. Link to invention. Ask: who makes a new thing for the first time?
notes.va.explorer.n: Explore + -er. The final e drops. Show explorer cards or a map.
notes.va.instructor.n: Instruct + -or. An instructor teaches a skill. Compare with teacher and coach.
notes.va.collector.n: Collect + -or. Show the three words collect, collector, and collection together.
notes.va.excitement.n: Excite + -ment. The e stays. The -ment ending makes a noun that names the feeling.
notes.va.amusement.n: Amuse + -ment. Amusement is quieter than excitement; ask students to act both.
notes.va.agreement.n: Agree + -ment. Link to disagreement and the earlier word obedient: both are about following shared rules.
notes.va.treatment.n: Treat + -ment. Here it is medical care. Students may know the word treat as a snack; note the difference.
notes.va.collection.n: Collect + -ion. A collection is the group; a collector is the person. Draw both on the board.
notes.va.celebration.n: Celebrate + -ion. The e drops before -ion. Ask students to name a celebration and what it honors.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: "I see collector. I know collect means to bring things together. The ending -or means a person who does something. So a collector is a person who gathers things. In the story, Ben brings stones, so he is a collector."
discuss: Which word in this unit tells about a person? Which tells about a feeling?
How can one base word make many new words?
misconceptions: -er and -or are different endings for different meanings.
Adding -ment always makes a feeling word.
A collection and a collector are the same thing.
All words ending in -ion are verbs.
extend: Make a word web for one base verb with at least three new words.
Look in a book for words ending in -er, -or, -ment, or -ion and tell the base word.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the three base-and-ending sets two days later with a sort, and again at one week. Use thoughtful, region, and reunite when writing about people and places in the next lessons.

wida.oral: Partner A says a base verb; Partner B adds an ending to make a person or a thing and uses it in a sentence.
